docs.title: EAR Member Handbook
docs.text:
Ecosystem Action Research (EAR) provides participation pathways for individuals and organizations to investigate shared conditions, imagine desirable futures, and identify themes for strategic development in order to bring about a public interest internet. Our 2026 strategic objectives in the EAR charter center innovation within the AT Protocol ecosystem.

The EAR project is made possible by collective members with the leadership and accountability of our project committee, strategic foresight and collective decision-making facilitatd by the steering group, and member services provided by operations. EAR is a project of the Raft Foundation.

docs.title: Intended audience
docs.text:
The EAR handbook’s primary audience is EAR members. The handbook is publicly available for others who may find it useful. The goal is to give members clarity and context while sharing our structures and practices with those interested.

The handbook may link to internal documents which contain more up-to-date information.

docs.title: How to contribute
docs.text:
All are welcome to suggest changes or raise a concern about handbook content by email. EAR members may open issues in Github to discuss content updates and additions. Pull requests are also welcome.

docs.title: General terms
docs.text: • Public interest technology: “Public Interest Technology refers to the study and application of technology expertise to advance the public interest in a way that generates public benefits and promotes the public good, particularly for those members of our society least well served historically and today by existing systems and policies.” — PIT Lab, Stanford

docs.title: Organizational structure
docs.text:
• Steering: defines and protects EAR’s commitments
  • Services: the resource generation and distribution layer to enable autonomous work.
  • Programs: EAR-supported initiatives that engage in action research and to foster cooperative research and imagination.

docs.title: Artifacts
docs.text:
• Resource: Resources provide important or load bearing context about EAR standard operating procedures. Resources make processes, structures, or rituals legible and accessible to EAR members.
  • Agreement: Agreements are policy documents that shape how we work together at EAR. The process for how we ratify and evolve agreements will be defined in a decisions agreement.
  • Guide: Guides explain how EAR members get stuff done. Guides are independent from agreements, in that they provide examples and standard operating procedure examples that make it easy to pick up and apply policy defined in agreements to everyday scenarios.
  • Proposal: Proposals are conversation starters that diagnose a problem, describe an opportunity area, and propose both guiding policy and an action plan to make it happen. The purpose of a proposal is to solicit feedback and collaboration to introduce a new policy, spark a change, or evolve how we work.

docs.title: Who we serve
docs.text:
We engage with a broad range of people building, organizing, and working in public interest internet technology. We also engage with people who want to contribute but aren’t sure how. To that end…

We primarily engage with, support, and equip …

  • Technologists and knowledge workers including architects, designers, developers, subject-matter experts
  • Organization leaders and business owners
  • Community organizers

… so that they may better serve:

  • Everyday new and returning users
  • Trust and safety staff
  • Creators or “power users” such activists, artists, journalists, small businesses
  • Communities such as friends, family, movements, interest-groups, neighbors, etc.

This means that we conduct research with a diverse range of audiences, participants, and allies. Interested? Send us a message!.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
We respond to all relevant inquiries. If your inquiry matches up with our charter, an EAR member will schedule a time to meet and discuss your needs. In the meantime, we suggest you read our personal conduct and research & imagination agreements.

During our discovery call we’ll ask you a series of questions about your goals, the challenges you’re facing, and how you might like to engage with EAR. After the call, we’ll share a follow up communication with a summary of our discussion and next steps, if appropriate.

docs.title: Share an inquiry, challenge, or opportunity
docs.text: We welcome research and event inquiries at [email address]. We will review each inquiry and respond usually within 2-4 weeks. Note: Inquiries are subject to availability, sponsorship, and alignment with EAR’s charter.

docs.title: Charter agreement
docs.text: The EAR charter informs internal policy, decision-making, and operations.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Ecosystem Action Research (EAR) exists to help make public interest internet technology legible, usable, and practical for everyday people around the globe.

docs.title: Vision
docs.text: We envision an information ecosystem where people and communities interact online through systems supported by socially responsible business models, democratic stewardship, and interoperable infrastructure, unmediated by oligopoly interests.

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: In service of this vision, we facilitate action research and strategic innovation with individuals and organizations building technology that gives people and communities agency over their online social identity, connections, activity, and content feeds.

docs.title: Who we are
docs.text:
EAR is a collective made up of members who believe in the potential of public interest technology to improve the options on the menu for everyday people. We do not gate-keep access based on bias to action, prior experience, or academic or professional credentials. We believe in creating an environment where anyone participating in good faith can explore and learn together.

We encourage all interested in this type of volunteer work to apply to join. We onboard members by invitation in cohorts, so please be advised that it may take some time for us to review your application and get back to you.

We do not have any paid or full time roles available at this time.

docs.title: Whom we serve
docs.text:
We believe a thriving public interest internet ecosystem ought to appeal to and empower the people who contribute to and steward internet communities every day. To that end…

We engage with, support, and equip …

  • Technologists and knowledge workers including architects, designers, trust and safety staff, developers, subject-matter experts
  • Organization leaders and business owners
  • Community organizers

… so that they may better serve:

  • Everyday new and returning users of public interest internet tech
  • Workers
  • Creators or “power users” such activists, artists, journalists, small businesses
  • Communities such as friends, family, movements, interest-groups, neighbors, etc.

docs.title: 1. Access‑centered, emergent practice
docs.text:
An access centered practice moves people into spaces that they don’t normally have access to. It breaks down barriers. We recognize that people have a variety of needs, interests, and backgrounds. Because of this, we include people who otherwise may feel excluded, and we emphasize mutual learning across community boundaries.

Emergent strategy comes out of struggle. Challenges and obstacles that communities, individuals, and groups experience every day hold real world data and relational context we can all learn from. We look for inspiration, knowledge, and expertise in places that are too-often overlooked—with an aim to co-design solutions with the people who use and rely on technology every day to communicate with people they care about.

docs.title: 2. Individual choice and collective self-determination
docs.text:
Technology built in the public interest expands the options on the menu for everyday people rather than restricting them. We prioritize methods, policies, and programs that put participant consent, choice, and autonomy first, including participants as stakeholders when distributing research findings and insights. Individual choice and collective self-determination also apply to how we work.

Our code of conduct sets the expectation that we actively repair harm. It’s to this end we ask EAR members to: show up in good relationship; actively share power; center people, not just perspectives; treat lived experience as expertise; take responsibility when we cause harm; pace ourselves and protect others’ ability to do the same; and protect participant privacy.

docs.title: 3. Intercommunal partnership
docs.text:
Coalition building requires moving beyond comfort zones to identify shared values, incentives, and objectives. Movement building requires some level of learning with and working alongside people we may disagree with about a bunch of things. Building alternatives to incumbent oligopolies requires multiple approaches and many protocols and standards.

The past, present, and future of communication online is shaped by the same incentive and communication structures that define how organizations work. Organizations seeking market domination operate differently than organizations that center partnership. A cooperative approach to market competition becomes possible when organizations prioritize intercommunal partnership while respecting autonomy.

docs.title: 4. Legibility and legitimacy building
docs.text:
People gather where their communities gather. For internet technology to be in the public interest, it must be approachable, accessible, and understandable by everyday people around the globe. We prioritize work and resource allocation to serve the development and maturity of the institutions, products, services, and communities working to implement decentralized technology with broad appeal, beyond privileged audiences.

Past platform shifts built momentum by developing trustful relationships with users, standards organizations, and markets. New markets take time to grow sustainably, and there’s much to learn from prior paradigm shifts, established industry expertise, and movements. With this in mind, we prioritize choices that invite participation from experts alongside participant observers, community members, and organizational leaders to build collective market legitimacy.

docs.title: 5. Interdependence and reciprocity
docs.text:
Our information ecosystem is influenced by and contributes to different types of ecosystem dynamics, network effects, incentive structures, and shifting norms. We believe that navigating complex environments requires recognizing the importance of interdependent relationships, acknowledging our assumptions, considering multiple perspectives, and including others before making irreversible decisions.

Similarly, we accept that the future of the internet will be multi-protocol, multicultural, and dependent on open access rather than beholden to walled gardens controlled by closed platforms. Rather than picking one technology to rule them all, or the success of a single community at the expense of others, we believe it is preferable to partner across contexts to see where we can identify shared values and goals to work toward.

docs.title: 6. Justice and equity over urgency or supremacy
docs.text:
Decision-making that centers justice and equity stands in the face of performative urgency, supremacy, and domination politics. We believe it’s ok for things to take longer than expected. If public interest innovation is to empower oppressed and marginalized communities on the fringes, it ought to include them in the process.

This commitment requires paying careful attention to relationships, even when there are ever-present incentives to move fast. We want to create space to move deliberately and with intention so that others may participate in—and benefit from—the sense-making we engage in together. Finally, we are not beholden to a single corporation or organization. Rather, we include stakeholders who are affected by—not just responsible for funding—our work.

docs.title: Positioning statement
docs.text: EAR provides participation pathways for individuals and organizations to investigate shared conditions, imagine desirable futures, and identify themes for strategic development in order to bring about a public interest internet.

docs.title: 2026 objectives
docs.text:
1 year objectives that ladder up to the 5 year mission and vision. We will revisit and update objectives each year.

Our year one objectives center the Authenticated Transfer (AT) Protocol technology ecosystem. We are open to working with groups working with other technologies in the future. Interested in working with or supporting us? Let us know! (link to form)

  1. Facilitate collective sense-making around key AT network ecosystem dynamics including what users value in common user experience scenarios and how the ecosystem is perceived.
  2. Elevate the capacity of AT network community support systems by developing visibility and shared understanding of the experience of builders, creators, community organizers, founders, trust & safety staff, subject-matter experts, and end-users in the ecosystem.
  3. Equip product, trust & safety, user experience, and engineering teams building on AT network technology with shared understanding and language around common concepts, patterns, user needs, and tasks relevant to the ecosystem.
  4. Provide resources, research artifacts, and reference materials to enable a diverse range of organizations and individuals to participate in the emergent ecosystem enabled by AT network technology.

docs.title: Comms Strategy Summary
docs.text:
EAR’s external voice follows a polyvocal strategy in which personal, project, and program accounts can communicate about EAR’s work directly, in their own voice, without routing through a central editorial process or authority. The official EAR accounts roles are narrower: carrying organizational information and shared decisions, and amplifying work happening from within and elsewhere, rather than being a central external voice.

EAR’s external communication follows the same patterns as our internal decision-making: radiate intent, invite advice, act without permission and with trust and consent. Most communication, whether it’s a participant’s personal knowledge, experience, or work, doesn’t need a check-in before it’s shared.

The Strategic Communications circle is the working group that stewards this approach. Day-to-day execution, including content calendar and publishing cadence, is facilitated by the Editorial service and anyone within EAR can participate in molding and aligning with emerging narratives through their own efforts.

For more details on our communications strategy and how to participate, see the Communication guide and our (draft) EAR Communications Strategy document.

docs.title: Update types and cadence
docs.text:
Update Type Content Cadance Biweekly steering update Internal Meeting notes Every 2 weeks, synced to steering meetings Organizational updates Internal Higher level updates about the overall activities of the organization Every 6 weeks Organizational updates External Higher level updates about the overall activities of the organization Every 6 weeks, 1-2 weeks after internal

Internal updates inform public comms:

  • The biweekly steering update may have specific todos or line items that may call for/be opportunities for public engagement, either through the EAR accounts or participant accounts
  • Internal organizational updates can be seen as drafts for public communications. This means the internal updates can double as feedback mechanisms for what we publish publicly.
  • We can set a lag time for feedback in the cadence for internal comment before external publishing, which means that external comms have been vetted twice before going public (once while being written for EAR internal, second by EAR internal participants.)

How the EAR social media profiles and feeds are staffed, accessed, and paced is TBD. The Strategic Communications circle is responsible for evolving the practices and policies around how official assets are used.

docs.title: External updates
docs.text:
We set a lag time for feedback in the cadence for internal comment before external publishing, which means that external comms have been vetted twice before going public (once while being written for EAR internal, second by EAR internal participants).

Beyond this, we can establish guidelines, process, etc for other kinds of public comms, but otherwise we want to keep official EAR comms to a minimum other than to amplify voices in the community as opportunities and needs arise.

docs.title: Financials agreement
docs.text:
EAR operates with financial transparency and accountability, with processes in place to manage funds, support collaborative programs, and ensure the economic sustainability of our mission.

The EAR project committee manages funds through the Ecosystem Action Research Open Collective.

docs.title: Types of funds
docs.text: Money held by EAR falls into two categories. Core fund, collaborative funds.

docs.title: Core fund
docs.text: The core fund is controlled by the project committee. These funds are used for operational expenses and providing economic runway for EAR.

docs.title: Collaborative funds
docs.text: Collaborative funds may be allocated to specific people for time and materials in order to finance approved programs, based on a transparent program development, scoping, budgeting, and approval process.

docs.title: Income
docs.text: EAR may receive income from companies, individuals, grant makers or other entities.

docs.title: General-purpose gifts
docs.text: General purpose gifts to EAR are allocated at the discretion of the project committee to either core operating costs or program-specific endeavors

docs.title: Program-specific gifts
docs.text: Gifts may be earmarked for a specific program. If that’s the case, we’ll prioritize spending earmarked funds for their specified purpose—if a program ends before all funds earmarked for that program have been exhausted, remaining funds will be moved into the core fund.

docs.title: Membership is free
docs.text: There are no membership fees required to participate in EAR.

docs.title: Spending
docs.text: Money spent by EAR may include fixed costs, discretionary costs, and emergency costs.

docs.title: Collaborative funding process
docs.text: A collaborative funding process must have a facilitator who is responsible for the process. Ensure rules for the process are clearly documented, reviewed, and approved by the project committee. Budgeting for the process is done in a transparent manner. Driving the process Reporting outcomes to the EAR group Entities that receive the funds are held accountable Funds may only be allocated to a collaborative funding program if the process has been clearly documented and approved by the project committee. If no such rules have previously been defined, a proposal must be developed and socialized for review and approval with the project committee.

docs.title: Financial accountability and transparency
docs.text: Financial matters are the responsibility of the project committee. The committee ensures that all transactions are documented in the EAR Open Collective with corresponding proposal, budget, and forecast documentation.

docs.text: Anyone can schedule internal meetings and events. See the schedule a meeting or event guide for an overview of tools and tips for scheduling.

docs.title: Meetings

docs.title: Events

All proposed external events must be cleared with the steering group before discussing publicly.

External events are supported by the Convening working group. To schedule an external event, Post in #convening in Zulip with what you need or would like to accomplish. Include:

  • the type of gathering
  • approximate date and duration
  • who's attending

  • any facilitation, access, or moderation requirements.

For external events needing a Luma or Atmosphere listing, flag this in your request. Luma admin access is currently held by Christian, Bryan, and Lyre.

docs.title: Expectations for members
docs.text: EAR members are expected to agree to the EAR charter, abide by the EAR code of conduct, and participate in good faith. We all experience life differently, and seasons come and go. Member ability to contribute may ebb and flow as seasons change. It’s OK to hang back and observe to find the right thing to contribute to. It’s encouraged to get involved in small ways, engage in discussion, and learn from and with your peers.

docs.title: Leaving EAR
docs.text:
It’s equally important to feel comfortable stepping away if that’s what’s best for you. If you have made commitments to one or more working groups, please notify your group or [email address] if you intend to step away. We welcome members participating as they are able, even if it’s for a limited amount of time.

docs.title: Personal conduct agreement
docs.text: Agreement Version 01, updated May 9th, 2026

docs.title: EAR is a collective
docs.text:
Ecosystem Action Research (EAR) is a community-run research collective. EAR is fiscally hosted by Raft Foundation which means Raft handles our financial administration and we operate under their organization. EAR does action research: We plan, act, learn, and repeat. We do this together, in public, in service of an ecosystem we believe in.

You do not need to be an expert in anything to participate in EAR. If you are here as a research participant, this document explains the norms that govern how we treat you and each other. This code of conduct applies to everyone in relationship with EAR. This includes contributors, volunteers, contractors, and research participants. This applies to all spaces where EAR work happens including but not limited to our Zulip, on bluesky, our blog, video calls, workshops, and any other venue where we gather under the EAR name.

As we are a project of the Raft Foundation we also inherit the Raft’s values. This document builds on that foundation and addresses what is specific to how EAR works. It does not replace the Raft Foundation values.

This is a living document. It will change as our community grows and as we learn.

docs.title: Unacceptable behaviors include, but are not limited to
docs.text:
The following behaviors are not acceptable in EAR spaces, regardless of intent:

  • Discrimination or demeaning conduct based on gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, disability, neurodivergence, age, class, caste, religion or lack of religion, immigration or citizenship status, national origin, or language
  • Racist or otherwise racially demeaning language or conduct
  • Making threats or encouraging others to violence or harm, using words or imagery
  • Causing someone to fear for their safety such as through stalking, following, or intimidation
  • Nonconsensual or unwelcome physical contact or sexual attention
  • Homophobia, transphobia, or biphobia, including deadnaming, misgendering, or questioning the validity of someone’s identity
  • Publication of private communications without consent
  • Ableism, including dismissing access needs as inconvenient or excessive
  • Dismissing lived experience as insufficient evidence or as less valid than formal credentials
  • Taking credit for, misrepresenting, or using someone else’s work without attribution or consent
  • Retaliation for raising a concern or making a report under this code

This list is not exhaustive. The standard is whether a behavior creates harm, exclusion, or fear.

docs.title: Expected behaviors include, but are definitely not limited to
docs.text:
EAR asks more than the absence of harm. We are working toward actively repairing prior harm, not just avoiding producing it.

Show up in relationship. When your capacity or commitments change, say so early. Silence is harder in collaboration than a hard conversation. We coordinate on trust and trust requires communication. The responsibility for making this norm safe and not penalizing people for stepping back, not placing coordination burden on those already carrying it most, sits with whoever holds coordination power, not with the person stepping back.

Actively share power. EAR contributors hold power over research participants. Long-tenured members hold power over newcomers. People with more technical fluency hold power over those without it. Name this when it shows up and make decisions to account for it.

Center people, not just perspectives. Actively make space for people whose voices are less centered by default. This applies to who we invite, how we facilitate, and in who holds leadership. Diverse perspectives are not enough if the people holding them are not present and empowered.

Treat lived experience as expertise. Someone’s direct experience of a system is evidence about that system.

Take responsibility when you cause harm. We will all make mistakes. The commitment is not to be perfect but to listen when someone tells you you caused harm, take it seriously, and repair what you can.

Pace yourself and protect others’ ability to do the same. This is volunteer work. Joy, rest, and rigorous care are not aspirational. They are how we sustain this over time. Do not treat overextension as dedication.

Keep internal information internal. Internal transparency is essential to how we work. Public transparency is powerful and must be handled with care. Privacy protects the people most at risk including research participants who have shared things in confidence and contributors whose personal situations are not public. When in doubt, ask before sharing.

docs.title: Research participants
docs.text:
If you are participating in an EAR interview, workshop, or other research activity, additional protections apply to you.

Your participation must be:

  • Voluntary. You can decline to answer anything, or leave at any time, without penalty.
  • Informed. You will know what the research is for, who will see your contributions, and how they will be used before you agree to participate.
  • Specific. Your consent applies to the scope described to you. We will not use your contributions for other purposes without asking again.
  • Revertible. You can withdraw consent after the fact. If you do, we will remove your contributions from material under our control.

docs.title: Reporting guidelines
docs.text:
If you experience or witness behavior that violates this code of conduct, reach out to: Christian Jacobs or Taurean Bryant in Zulip or by email.

Reports will be received with care and confidentiality.

docs.title: Software systems
docs.text:
EAR members rely on software systems to share information and collaborate online. The software we choose to use day-to-day can impact our ability to collaborate effectively, who is enabled to participate, our operating budget, and switching costs.

Members can request software systems support in Zulip or via email.

docs.title: Selecting software systems
docs.text:
Factors to consider when evaluating software that may be maintained by members of the EAR collective include:

Qualities we look for

  • Data sovereignty — who owns and controls access to the data?
  • Ease of migration — can we realistically move our data to a new provider?
  • Usability — how flexible is the system in making the information legible to me?
  • Digital accessibility — how inclusive is the tool to people with various levels of ability or disability?
  • Attention — does the system respect my attention as a volunteer, or does it demand more of me than I have to give in order to get value from it?
  • Justice — How does the company treat individuals and organizations with less resources? Do they care? Do they have programs to lift folks up? How does the organization treat its people?
  • Ease of onboarding — Can someone with limited bandwidth start working in a reasonable amount of time?
  • Pricing model — is the pricing model practical for the number of members who ought to have access?
  • Labor practices
  • Maintenance cost — Will the cost of this tool have a downstream influence on deciding who can contribute?
  • Admin labor —
  • Software maturity — (stable + supported?)

Things we weigh carefully:

  • Per-user software costs

docs.text:

  1. Programs 1.1 Upcoming program review, feedback, go/no-go 1.2 Potential program preplanning/development and proposals
  2. Policy and communications 2.1 Policy 2.2 Communications
  3. Horizon scanning: What other challenges or opportunities are on the horizon? 3.1 Within EAR 3.2 Across ecosystems we work with (starting with AT Protocol)
  4. Highlights & Next steps 4.1 Reflecting on and summarizing emergent concerns 4.2 Communicating progress and upcoming opportunities to the EAR community and strategic comms working group for external comms.

docs.title: Participate in steering
docs.text: All EAR members with interest in shaping near-term strategy are invited and encouraged to contribute to steering conversations and decisions. To participate in Steering, join the next bi-weekly Steering Meeting Sync in Luma.

docs.title: EAR Decisions agreement
docs.text:
EAR is a trusted network of people working together to help make public interest internet technology legible, usable, and practical for everyday people. We believe members should make their own decisions, with care for others inside and outside the collective.

Decisions are made through consent and participation. Members are expected to seek advice and include others before making high-stakes decisions, and take steps to ensure serious objections are respected when they arise.

Not every decision carries the same weight. Decisions that set precedent, commit resources, or have greater consequence should be informed by more voices and have more time to discuss before moving forward.

In practice this means making decisions visible inside EAR when considering: Is this good enough for now, and safe enough to try? Multiple members are included in every major decision. Proposals move when they're workable, even if it isn't everyone's first choice, unless they are blocked based on a serious objection.

docs.title: Radiate intent
docs.text: Sharing early and often creates an invitation to collaborate. Communicate what you're about to do, before you do it, in the relevant Zulip channel or wherever the work already lives, so anyone affected has a chance to flag something early. No good proposal emerges fully formed from a singular perspective, and we're better when we work together.

docs.title: Invite advice
docs.text:
At EAR, you can act without asking permission first. This freedom comes with a responsibility: make sure the people a decision affects, and the people who know the subject best, have had a chance to inform your action before it moves forward. Seeking advice this way is a means of practicing accountability before the fact and respecting the lived experience and expertise of the people around you, and it's what lets even a decision not everyone agrees with keep the group's trust.

Before moving on a proposal:

  • Share questions, problem areas, and opportunity spaces in topical channels in Zulip. Ask if anyone may have expertise, or may know someone with expertise.
  • Consider adding subject-matter experts and stakeholders tables to proposals, and invite people to add to it.

docs.title: Gather broader input
docs.text:
Sometimes advice from a few people isn't enough to know where a group stands, especially on something that touches a lot of people or reopens a disagreement that may have surfaced previously. In such cases it's worth checking the temperature of the wider group before moving forward, using techniques such as polling or group interviews. This doesn't replace the consent process, but it does tell you where people are before you ask for it.

For tools that support this, see the Software Systems Agreement.

docs.title: Proposal and discussion
docs.text:
Everyone is encouraged to raise discussions and proposals with a clear course of action or resolution pathway. If you'd like help getting clarity or refining a proposal, don't be afraid to start with a rough draft and invite feedback and collaboration.

Once a proposal has circulated and had time to gather advice, whoever raised it checks the group for objections. This is where participants can weigh in by responding with one of the following four positions.

Position Meaning Agree You’re happy with the proposal Abstain You’re happy for the group to decide without you. Disagree There might be a better alternative, but you’re willing to go along with the group’s decision. Block You have serious objections and believe there is serious risk if this initiative moves forward as-is.

docs.title: Blocking a proposal
docs.text:
A block is different from a disagreement. Disagree means you'd have chosen differently but can live with the group's call. Block means you believe the proposal poses risk to the group, or runs against EAR's purpose, mission, or vision. Held to that standard, blocking carries weight precisely because it's used sparingly, not as a stand-in for personal preference.

A single block stops a proposal from moving forward as written. That's a significant responsibility to carry as a blocking contributor: block because you see risk to the group, not because you would have preferred a different approach. And it's everybody's responsibility, not just the blocker's, to work through a block in good faith and with respect for each other.

  • You don't have to propose an alternative when you block. You will be asked to explain your concern in a timely way so the group can understand it.
  • Take the time to help others understand what the proposal is trying to achieve, and why you believe it doesn't get there safely.

A block reopens the conversation rather than ending it: the proposal gets reworked, or the concern gets addressed, until the block is no longer needed. The result is a stronger decision than the one first proposed.

docs.title: Decision culture and practice
docs.text:
How we make decisions is inseparable from how we treat each other while making them. For the culture and principles that ground this work, see the how we show up guide.

The two lists below name what we ask of each other in a decision.

docs.title: Bring yourself to a decision
docs.text:
• Share your views and opinions! If you’re in this group, your experience and perspective are valued.
  • Aim to be succinct and clear in your communication. This isn’t always how we show up, and that’s OK.
  • Invite participation and advice from others.
  • Learn from each other. Ask questions. Listen to understand, not to find fault.
  • Participate when you’re able and interested, even if your contributions are small.
  • Be prepared to evolve your thinking.
  • Embrace diverse perspectives and other approaches.
  • Ask for help if you’d like to engage more or are having trouble understanding an issue. You’re probably not alone.

docs.title: Make room for others
docs.text:
• Share early and often
  • Involve people you don’t work with often
  • Make connections and develop professional working relationships
  • If you encounter conflict or confusion, consider holding a conversation to invite multiple perspectives and learn from the group
  • Facilitation is usually the missing link; invite those to speak who haven’t spoken often, clarify and summarize points raised, suggest timing and next steps, encourage sharing advice and feedback.

docs.title: Decision template
docs.text: A formal template is forthcoming. Until then, log a decision where the work already lives: post it in the relevant Zulip channel with enough context for someone to understand what was decided and why, and make sure anyone it affects hears about it directly rather than finding out later (this is what we mean by radiating intent).

docs.title: Decision types and timelines
docs.text: Type Description Criteria Protocol Timeframe Examples Informal Each of us make decisions every day that shape how we show up internally and externally. Easily reversible. Share early and often and encourage cooperation. If you’re making your work visible and are able to share an understanding without identifying significant barriers or dependencies, you’re probably on the right track! Radiate intent. Invite feedback and advice. 3 working days. 5 encouraged. Day-to-day activities such as identifying problems and opportunities, experimenting with ways of working, or facilitating cooperation and collaboration. Formal From surfacing problems and opportunities to proposing a new program or function, everyone is encouraged to make and contribute to significant decisions. Reversible with risk or cost. Work with others to structure and iterate on a proposal. Invite diverse perspectives, obtain signoff from a few others—familiar and unfamiliar with the proposal. Radiate intent. Invite feedback and advice. Share with steering for visibility and advice. 5 working days. 10 encouraged. Brand: using EAR’s brand publicly. Relationships: commitments with individuals or entities (such as sending membership invitations, starting programs, or establishing partnerships). Tools and processes: setting up or modifying guides, tools, or software. Intellectual property: using EAR data or content. Money: spending collective funds. Policy-level Policy updates streamline decision-making and promote shared understanding. Sets a new course or precedent for the collective. Work with collaborators to draft and iterate on a proposal. Obtain sign of from a handful of others, including at least one project committee member. Radiate intent. Draft a proposal. Invite advice. Escalate to steering for visibility and advice. 5 working days. 10 encouraged. Introduce new agreements or make changes to existing agreements. Escalated There may be times when the wellbeing of the collective ought to be protected by reversing prior decisions to mitigate risk. Irreversible, at least in the near-term. Work with trusted thought-partners and a member of the project committee to address the issue. Radiate intent. Draft a proposal. Invite advice. Escalate to project committee for visibility, advice, or decision support. 10 working days. Removing a team member or project from the group.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The EAR community is a gathering place for members and those we partner with to help make public interest internet technology legible, usable, and practical for everyday people1. We engage in this work through a combination of action research and imagination tracks. Research and imagination programming provide pathways to investigate shared conditions, reflect on the past, and explore desirable futures together.

While all of this is in service of innovation, we intentionally create a space for imagination in service of innovation, rather than attempting to innovate on our own. This is in part because in order to realize desirable futures, we must first imagine them. There are many people capable of and involved in direct action. Indirect action is necessary to help create the conditions necessary to inform direct action with plural, inclusive, and effective contexts.

docs.title: Action Research
docs.text:
People are more likely to help shape what’s next when they are active participants in exploring and improving situations affecting them.

We investigate current-state conditions and emerging opportunity spaces through the lenses of participatory and collaborative action research. This means we invite participation from those affected and collaboration with those who bring subject matter expertise and real world experience related to the matters we explore.

docs.title: Imagination
docs.text:
While some of our research explores current-state conditions and near-term opportunities, a key factor in shaping innovation is to imagine a range of potential futures together. Imagination programs bring people together to reflect on the past and explore possibilities that may appear possible, plausible, probable, or preferable.

“By being very specific about the things we can imagine in the future, we sharpen our powers of discernment about what we want and do not want, identifying what dynamics are life-sustaining versus life-draining.”

—Ruha Benjamin, Imagination: A Manifesto

It’s our hope that through collective imagination we help give people an opportunity to participate in and contribute to the conversation about what a public interest internet might look like.

docs.title: EAR objectives 2026
docs.text:
Research & imagination programs at EAR ladder up to the one year objectives outlined in our founding charter, reviewed quarterly by the steering group, and ratified yearly by the project committee. To focus our work, programs proposed outside of or beyond the bounds of our one year objectives will not be considered by the steering group.

From the charter:

  1. Facilitate collective sense-making around key AT network ecosystem dynamics including what users value in common user experience scenarios and how the ecosystem is perceived.
  2. Elevate the capacity of AT network community support systems by developing visibility and shared understanding of the experience of builders, creators, community organizers, founders, trust & safety staff, subject-matter experts, and end-users in the ecosystem.
  3. Equip product, trust & safety, user experience, and engineering teams building on AT network technology with shared understanding and language around common concepts, patterns, user needs, and tasks relevant to the ecosystem.
  4. Provide resources, research artifacts, and reference materials to enable a diverse range of organizations and individuals to participate in the emergent ecosystem enabled by AT network technology.

Each research project starts with group inquiry. The input of group inquiry can simply be a question or a statement, and a scheduled session with an agenda to begin together. Each research question can then be explored using separate, focused research tracks. As research projects are executed and findings and insights are surfaced, these insights may be fed into research reports related to an opportunity theme or topic.

docs.title: Restorative justice
docs.text: EAR is made up of conversations between people. Our work is about relationships. Disagreement and some level of conflict are part of any cooperative environment. We ask all EAR participants to recognize these guidelines for resolving serious conflict.

docs.title: 1. Contemplate conflict
docs.text:
• Take time to process if you feel confused, overwhelmed, or agitated.
  • Consider uncertainties or possible misunderstandings, including different cultural and life experiences.
  • Review relevant policy documents or guides.

If you’ve considered the experience and decide it may be harassment or abuse, please consult our personal conduct policy.

docs.title: 2. Invite conversation
docs.text:
If you’re unable to resolve a conflict, invite conversation. The sooner the better!

  • If you feel able and safe to, directly discuss your concerns with the person you are in conflict with
  • Otherwise, see Conflict resolution support

docs.title: 3. Develop a plan
docs.text:
• Foster inclusive dialogue by sharing ideas, asking clarifying questions, and responding to others’ ideas. Identify wants and needs. Make offers and requests.
  • Develop points of agreement to facilitate progress.
  • Propose plans to treat conflict in a mutually satisfactory way.
  • Follow up later to discuss progress.

docs.title: Conflict resolution support
docs.text: Again, if you’re unsure how to proceed, feel unsafe, or are experiencing harassment or abuse, please consult our personal conduct policy. If you currently feel unsafe in EAR’s communication channels, please email [].

docs.title: How we show up
docs.text: EAR members are asked to foster a collaborative, resilient environment by aligning with core values of trust, transparency, and presence.

docs.title: EAR project values
docs.text: The EAR project’s values statements are listed in our charter.

docs.title: Inspired by…
docs.text:
EAR is a project of the Raft foundation. As the EAR collective emerged, we’ve been in conversation together around the Raft Foundation’s values and secondary principles. If you’re an EAR member, please review the Raft values as they also reflect how we’d like to work together within the EAR project.

We are also inspired by adrienne maree brown’s principles of Emergent Strategy:

  1. Small is good, small is all. (The large is a reflection of the small.)
  2. Change is constant. (Be like water.)
  3. There is always enough time for the right work.
  4. There is a conversation in the room that only these people at this moment can have. Find it.
  5. Never a failure, always a lesson.
  6. Trust the People. (If you trust the people, they become trustworthy.)
  7. Move at the speed of trust. Focus on critical connections more than critical mass — build the resilience by building the relationships.
  8. Less prep, more presence.
  9. What you pay attention to grows.

docs.title: In practice
docs.text:
From our code of conduct, expected behaviors include, but are not limited to:

Show up in relationship. When your capacity or commitments change, say so early. Silence is harder in collaboration than a hard conversation. We coordinate on trust and trust requires communication. The responsibility for making this norm safe and not penalizing people for stepping back, not placing coordination burden on those already carrying it most, sits with whoever holds coordination power, not with the person stepping back.

Actively share power. EAR contributors hold power over research participants. Long-tenured members hold power over newcomers. People with more technical fluency hold power over those without it. Name this when it shows up and make decisions to account for it.

Center people, not just perspectives. Actively make space for people whose voices are less centered by default. This applies to who we invite, how we facilitate, and in who holds leadership. Diverse perspectives are not enough if the people holding them are not present and empowered.

Treat lived experience as expertise. Someone’s direct experience of a system is evidence about that system.

Take responsibility when you cause harm. We will all make mistakes. The commitment is not to be perfect but to listen when someone tells you you caused harm, take it seriously, and repair what you can.

Pace yourself and protect others’ ability to do the same. This is volunteer work. Joy, rest, and rigorous care are not aspirational. They are how we sustain this over time. Do not treat overextension as dedication.

Keep internal information internal. Internal transparency is essential to how we work. Public transparency is powerful and must be handled with care. Privacy protects the people most at risk including research participants who have shared things in confidence and contributors whose personal situations are not public. When in doubt, ask before sharing.

docs.title: Opportunities are everywhere
docs.text: Just because we can do something doesn't mean we should. A key function of EAR is bringing people together to discuss opportunities and transform shared understanding of potential opportunities based on real-world problems through multiple stages of discovery and conversation.

docs.title: Explore an opportunity
docs.text:
Each action research cycle begins with conversation to identify a preliminary diagnosis, gather data, and plan further inquiry. The following inputs are considered during exploration:

  • Landscape and motivation: What are the challenges and problems identified?
  • Participant stakeholders: Who is affected? What are their roles, needs, desires, challenges, pain points, and hopes for the future?
  • Opportunity: What are desirable outcomes of this inquiry?
  • Data sources: What data or research exists today that may be relevant?
  • Subject matter experts: What expertise or community of practice may add value to the line of inquiry? Who can be invited?
  • Scope: Describe a scenario and various situations to focus the effort.
  • Assumptions, risks, constraints: What are the potential risks and mitigating factors?
  • Activities, deliverables and timeline: Identify key milestones, touch points, and deliverables. Time box the effort.

You are welcome to start an opportunity summary to kick off an exploration process for a specific opportunity area. We recommend that you schedule a kick off call either with a workshop format to surface the above, or to review an existing draft. Seeking advice and participation from EAR members is a good way to incorporate multiple perspectives early.

docs.title: Public relations
docs.text:

docs.title: Start a research project
docs.text:

If you’ve already started the process, bring a 1-2 page opportunity summary, project proposal, research plan, or doc of your choice to the #Steering group to seek advice. If you’d like help putting together a document, don’t be afraid to ask!

Anyone can start a project internally—whether that project is in line with our charter, objectives, and values will determine whether EAR is able to support or endorse the project publicly. Formal project proposals will be approved or rejected with feedback within 10 business days (two weeks) of the proposal being shared with the steering group based on a poll as described in the decisions agreement.

docs.text: Use active voice, avoid passive voice. Write in clear, plain language, and avoid jargon. Use positive statements rather than negative statements. Break long paragraphs into two or three short, concise sentences.

docs.title: Github

Github allows many contributors to all work on a single project. It has a system for storing files and proposing changes to them in a managed way, based on the open source git project.

All files that make up this handbook (will) live in a Github repository (or “repo”): https://github.com/ecosystemactionresearch/handbook

If you have a Github account, you can draft updated versions of the handbook and let people comment on your draft. You make a “pull request” to request that repo maintainers merge your changes into the canonical version of the handbook, the “main” version.

Github accounts are free. If you need help using git, see the #Software and tools channel and we’ll help you get sorted.

#Ops_editorial in Zulip

docs.title: Internal document release process
docs.text:
Every internal and external document version must include a change log and list of contributors.

  • Change log
  • Contributors

docs.title: Guiding policy
docs.text:
• Two or more people ought to own responsibility for a document.
  • Accountable (primary)
  • Responsible (secondary, etc.)
  • While everyone’s feedback is welcome, our goal isn’t that we need every single person involved to give a go or no-go. What might a number of people to determine a stop vs a go may be important
  • Traffic lights: green yellow red
  • Provide deadline at least [X] business days to review/approve object, share/boost in a Zulip channel (see decisions agreement)
  • Those accountable and responsible should seek feedback.
  • Everyone can give feedback, authoritative votes falls to whom (plural) is responsible
  • How do we ratify that this is done and official (see decisions agreement)

docs.title: Storing final versions of policy documents
docs.text:
• Publishing workflow
  • Track in a versioned environment
  • We want to be able to track change history, who’s involved/attribution

docs.title: Informal docs
docs.text: All EAR members are encouraged to create and circulate internal documents, RFCs, etc.

docs.title: Editorial
docs.text:
Material for external release (separate process)

  • External EAR comms need to be reviewed and approved by the EAR steering group and project committee.

docs.title: Internal iteration
docs.text:
• Anyone can propose new things within the group.
  • Suggestion: Draft a quick proposal outlining the problem, opportunity, audience voice/tone and purpose/rough outline of why a policy document may provide value. Circulate it for informal review. If you’d like, reach out to a colleague(s) for private review before sharing in a public channel.

Editorial is subject to the operations agreement.
